title: Syllabus
section: What Does This Class Look Like?
text:
What Does This Class Look Like?

Class Format
We meet once a week for three hours. Each class period is built around a central theme, and our time is split between lecture, live coding, and hands-on lab work — expect the balance to shift toward lab time as the semester goes on and the NBRC project takes over. I’ll build in a break (or two) to divide the three hours into distinct chunks.


Attendance Policy
You are required to attend class. Put simply, class is better — and your project team is more functional — when everyone shows up. Starting in Week 2, I will take attendance every class period. Everyone gets one free absence. Beyond that, absences will cost you points on your participation & attendance grade. If you know you’ll miss a class, give me a heads-up in advance rather than after the fact.


General Classroom Expectations
My goal as your instructor is to be supportive and build a learning environment where you can thrive. Your role as a student is to actively engage with the material, contribute to your project team, manage your time well, and embrace opportunities for hands-on practice — this is a lab-heavy course, and you learn R by writing R, not by watching it get written. You’re in charge of your own learning, but you’re never doing it alone.

Use of Generative AI Tools
Students are expected to use all available tools — including generative AI — to help them succeed in this course. Some of the evaluation in this course focuses on the soundness of programming, and AI tools may be genuinely helpful there. However, other evaluation is assessed visually and orally (in-class presentations, code walkthroughs, design critique), so over-reliance on AI is not recommended — you will need to be able to explain and defend your own work.

title: Syllabus
text:
Communication
If you need to reach me digitally, email is best. I follow a “one business day” rule for responding to student email: if you send something at 10am Monday, I have until 10am Tuesday to respond; if you send it at 6pm Friday, I have until start of business Tuesday. If more than a business day has passed, feel free to send a polite nudge.
Office hours are by appointment — email me and we’ll find a time. On most class days I’ll also stick around afterward for quick questions; please keep it brief if others are waiting.

title: University Policies & Resources

Lived Name and Pronoun Information
The UVM Directory includes fields for indicating your lived name and your pronouns. Lived names (preferred names, names in use) are names that an individual wants to be known by in the University community. Entering your pronouns is strongly encouraged to help create a more inclusive and respectful campus community. To update your information, log in to the UVM Directory. A preview box will let you see how this information will appear in other campus systems.

section: Intellectual Property / Prohibition on Sharing Academic Materials
text:
Intellectual Property / Prohibition on Sharing Academic Materials
Students are prohibited from publicly sharing or selling academic materials they did not author — for example, the class syllabus, outlines or presentations authored by the professor, practice questions, textbook excerpts, or other copyrighted class materials — and from sharing assessments such as homework or take-home exams. Violations are handled under UVM’s Intellectual Property policy and Code of Academic Integrity.

Important UVM Policies
Academic Integrity — Addresses plagiarism, fabrication, collusion, and cheating.
Code of Student Conduct — Outlines conduct expectations as well as students’ rights and responsibilities.
FERPA Rights Disclosure — Communicates students’ rights regarding access to, and privacy of, their educational records under the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) of 1974.
Final Exam Policy — Outlines expectations during final exams and explains the timing and process of the examination period.
Grade Appeals — The procedure to follow if you would like to contest a grade.
Grading — GPA calculation and general grading information.
Religious Holidays — Students have the right to practice the religion of their choice. Each semester, students should submit in writing to their instructor(s) — as early as possible, and at least one week before a documented religious holiday — the date(s) of any conflict or absence. Faculty must permit students who miss work or exams for religious observance to make up that work.

title: Community Partner Project
text:
Overview
The semester-long applied project is completed in partnership with the Northern Border Regional Commission (NBRC), a federal-state economic and community development commission serving rural northern Maine, New Hampshire, New York, and Vermont.
Students work in small teams. Each team analyzes a different domain area across NBRC’s full four-state territory (rather than each team covering a single state). All teams use a consistent structure so outputs are comparable and can be assembled into a unified product for NBRC.
